title: Cybersecurity: Red, Blue & Purple Teams
description: A beginner-friendly learning map of offensive security, defensive operations, purple-team validation, team collaboration, career paths, ethics, metrics, and AI's impact on cybersecurity.

root.label: Cybersecurity Teams
root.notes: Cybersecurity is a shared system for protecting an organization's mission, people, services, identities, and data. Red teams emulate credible attackers, blue teams prevent and respond to threats, and purple teaming turns their combined evidence into repeatable improvements. The goal is reduced business risk, not one team defeating another.

children.label: Shared Foundations
children.notes: Every security specialty rests on the same foundations: understanding systems, reasoning about risk, working safely, gathering evidence, and communicating clearly. Learn these before becoming dependent on particular products or tools.

children.label: Security Mental Models
children.notes: Learn the CIA triad of confidentiality, integrity, and availability; distinguish assets, threats, vulnerabilities, exposures, controls, likelihood, and impact; and use threat modeling to ask what can go wrong, what matters, and what evidence would change a decision.

children.label: Technical Foundations
children.notes: Study TCP/IP, routing, DNS, HTTP, TLS, email, VPNs, and packet capture; Linux and Windows processes, files, permissions, and services; identity, sessions, tokens, MFA, directories, IAM, and least privilege; web APIs, databases, cloud shared responsibility, containers, CI/CD, and software supply chains. Use Python, Bash, or PowerShell for small automations and Git for versioned work.

children.label: Ethics, Law & Authorization
children.notes: Security testing requires explicit authorization, a defined scope, and compliance with applicable law, contracts, organizational policy, privacy obligations, and third-party terms. If ownership, permission, or impact is unclear, stop and escalate. A home lab or intentionally vulnerable training environment is the correct place for beginner experimentation.

children.label: Operational Safety
children.notes: Use least privilege, isolated environments, designated test identities and data, safe payloads, backups, rollback plans, change control, synchronized timestamps, encrypted evidence, audit trails, emergency contacts, stop conditions, and verified cleanup. Minimize sensitive-data collection and preserve chain of custody when an investigation requires it.

children.label: Evidence & Communication
children.notes: Record assumptions, timestamps, sources, commands or actions, observations, confidence, business impact, and limitations. Write for both technical owners and decision-makers. Strong practitioners explain why a finding matters, how it can be reproduced safely, who should act, how to remediate it, and how the fix will be verified.

children.label: The Wider Security Ecosystem
children.notes: Red, blue, and purple are only part of cybersecurity. Governance, risk, compliance, audit, privacy, legal, product and application security, cloud security, architecture, IAM, vulnerability management, threat intelligence, awareness, physical security, business continuity, IT operations, software engineering, SRE, HR, communications, executives, asset owners, and vendors all contribute to security outcomes.

children.label: Red Team
children.notes: The red team is the authorized offensive function. It emulates realistic adversary behavior to test whether valuable objectives can be reached and whether people, processes, and technical controls work under pressure. Its purpose is evidence and improvement, never uncontrolled access or disruption.

children.label: Mission & Scope
children.notes: A red engagement starts with a business-relevant objective, such as demonstrating whether a protected data set or administrative capability can be reached. Stealth is used only when it serves the learning goal. Test depth, target assets, permitted techniques, exclusions, timing, evidence handling, cleanup, escalation, and success criteria must be agreed before execution.

children.label: Rules of Engagement
children.notes: The rules of engagement document written authorization, scope boundaries, allowed and forbidden actions, test windows, source addresses and accounts, production-safety limits, communications, incident deconfliction, emergency contacts, stop conditions, evidence handling, rollback, cleanup, and reporting expectations.

children.label: Scan vs Pentest vs Red Team
children.notes: A vulnerability scan identifies possible weaknesses, usually with automation. A penetration test validates and explains weaknesses in a defined technical scope. A red-team engagement chains techniques across people, process, and technology to pursue agreed objectives while measuring prevention, detection, and response. The terms are sometimes used loosely, so clarify the actual work.

children.label: Offensive Roles
children.notes: Titles overlap across organizations. Judge a role by its scope, expected evidence, safety responsibilities, and whether it focuses on assessment, emulation, research, or engineering.

children.label: Penetration Tester
children.notes: Validates vulnerabilities in a defined application, network, cloud, identity, mobile, API, or infrastructure scope; demonstrates impact safely; and produces reproducible findings and remediation advice.

children.label: Red-Team Operator
children.notes: Chains behaviors toward an agreed objective, manages operational security and infrastructure, coordinates safe execution, preserves evidence, and explains the attack path rather than reporting isolated weaknesses.

children.label: App, Identity & Cloud Specialist
children.notes: Examines source code, web applications, APIs, mobile clients, software supply chains, cloud configurations, trust relationships, IAM, Active Directory, hybrid identity, containers, and privilege boundaries.

children.label: Emulation Lead
children.notes: Translates threat intelligence and business concerns into engagement hypotheses, plans campaigns, coordinates operators and stakeholders, manages risk, and ensures the final narrative supports decisions.

children.label: Social Engineering Specialist
children.notes: Tests human and process controls only when explicitly authorized, with safeguards for privacy, welfare, escalation, and data handling. The objective is to improve systems and training, not shame individuals.

children.label: Engagement Lifecycle
children.notes: A disciplined red-team engagement is planned, observable to authorized controllers, reproducible enough to support remediation, and closed with verified cleanup.

children.label: Plan & Threat Model
children.notes: Identify critical assets and likely adversaries, agree objectives and rules of engagement, validate backups and escalation paths, choose appropriate techniques, and define the evidence needed to answer the security question.

children.label: Recon & Initial Access
children.notes: Within scope, understand the attack surface and trust relationships, identify viable entry paths, and perform controlled initial-access simulation. Use designated identities and safe payloads where possible.

children.label: Post-Access Objectives
children.notes: As permitted, validate execution, privilege escalation, credential access, persistence, discovery, lateral movement, collection, command and control, and controlled objective or exfiltration simulation. Execute only the minimum behavior needed to answer the hypothesis.

children.label: Cleanup, Report & Retest
children.notes: Remove artifacts and access, preserve and sanitize evidence, deconflict alerts or incidents, present an executive narrative and technical timeline, diagram attack paths, identify root causes and detection gaps, prioritize remediation, and support verification after fixes.

children.label: Skills & Tool Categories
children.notes: Understand protocols and systems before relying on automation. Offensive skills include reconnaissance, web and API testing, code review, network and identity attack paths, cloud and container boundaries, secure exploit validation, threat modeling, operational security, scripting, evidence capture, and report writing. Tool categories include intercepting proxies, scanners, packet analyzers, debuggers, directory graphing, cloud CLIs, and controlled command-and-control platforms used in labs or authorized engagements.

children.label: Outputs & Measures
children.notes: Useful outputs include an executive narrative, attack-path diagram, technical timeline, evidence, affected assets, observed controls, detection gaps, cleanup record, root-cause analysis, prioritized remediation, owners, and a retest plan. Useful measures include objectives reached, control failures, time to objective, detection and response observed, recurring paths, and remediation closure. Raw vulnerability counts or numbers of shells do not measure security value.

children.label: Blue Team
children.notes: The blue team reduces the likelihood and impact of incidents. It knows the environment, prevents avoidable exposure, maintains visibility, detects suspicious behavior, investigates and contains incidents, restores services safely, and converts lessons into stronger architecture and operations. Blue teaming is much broader than monitoring an alert queue.

children.label: Defensive Mission
children.notes: Know assets, identities, data, dependencies, exposure, normal behavior, business priorities, and recovery needs. Reduce attack paths with secure architecture, hardening, patching, least privilege, segmentation, resilient backups, and reliable change management. Maintain usable telemetry and rehearsed response authority so the organization can act under pressure.

children.label: Defensive Roles
children.notes: Defensive security spans monitoring, engineering, investigations, architecture, intelligence, and resilience. Team structures and tier labels differ, so focus on actual responsibilities.

children.label: SOC Analyst
children.notes: Triages alerts, gathers context, tests competing hypotheses, scopes affected assets and identities, documents evidence, escalates appropriately, and initiates or coordinates response.

children.label: Incident Response & DFIR
children.notes: Plans and leads containment, preserves evidence, reconstructs timelines, performs endpoint, cloud, identity, and network forensics, coordinates eradication and recovery, and produces lessons learned.

children.label: Threat Hunter
children.notes: Uses threat intelligence, environmental knowledge, and anomalies to form hypotheses and search for activity that existing detections may miss. A hunt should end with evidence, improved visibility, a new detection, or a documented learning.

children.label: Detection Engineer
children.notes: Designs, tests, versions, deploys, tunes, and maintains analytics and enrichment. Validates required data sources, known-positive and benign cases, alert routing, triage guidance, ownership, and regression tests.

children.label: Security Engineer & Architect
children.notes: Builds and operates controls, logging pipelines, IAM boundaries, secure platforms, segmentation, endpoint and cloud protections, automation, and resilient designs. Architecture reduces entire classes of incidents before alerts are needed.

children.label: Defensive Specialists
children.notes: Threat intelligence, malware analysis, vulnerability management, cloud security, IAM and privileged access, email security, data protection, security automation, and recovery engineering add depth to the defensive mission.

children.label: Defense & Incident Lifecycle
children.notes: Preparation is continuous. During an incident, defenders detect and analyze, contain the damage, eradicate causes, recover safely, monitor for recurrence, communicate with stakeholders, and turn the experience into changed controls and rehearsed playbooks.

children.label: Prepare & Prevent
children.notes: Classify assets and data, harden configurations, patch exposures, manage identities and secrets, collect relevant telemetry, train people, test backups, define decision authority, and rehearse incidents before they occur.

children.label: Detect & Analyze
children.notes: Correlate endpoint, network, identity, application, email, cloud, and threat context. Establish what happened, when it began, what is affected, how confident the assessment is, and what evidence would confirm or disprove it.

children.label: Contain, Eradicate & Recover
children.notes: Limit harm while preserving necessary evidence, remove persistence and root causes, rotate compromised credentials, restore from trusted states, validate services and data, monitor for recurrence, and communicate operational impact. Containment can disrupt the business, so authority and sequence should be predefined.

children.label: Lessons Learned
children.notes: Run a blameless review, compare expected and observed behavior, identify technical and organizational contributors, assign owners, update architecture, detections, playbooks, training, and recovery plans, and verify that agreed changes work.

children.label: Tools & Telemetry
children.notes: Common control categories include SIEM, EDR or XDR, network detection, IDS or IPS, email and web protections, IAM and PAM, vulnerability management, cloud posture and workload controls, backups, SOAR, and case management. The important capabilities are trustworthy data, time synchronization, normalization, retention, privacy, query fluency, data-source health, tested analytics, and clear operational ownership—not the product logo.

children.label: Outputs & Measures
children.notes: Outputs include detection rules, dashboards, hunts, cases, timelines, playbooks, automation, hardening baselines, incident reports, recovery tests, and control changes. Measures may include time to detect, acknowledge, contain, and recover; dwell time; precision and false-positive rates; data-source health; tested detection coverage; playbook success; recurrence; and recovery objectives. Pair speed with investigation quality and business impact.

children.label: Purple Team
children.notes: Purple teaming is a collaborative security practice that makes offensive and defensive learning explicit, rapid, and repeatable. It may be a dedicated function, a facilitator, or simply a working pattern between red and blue teams. It complements, but does not replace, independent assurance, penetration testing, architecture review, vulnerability management, or incident response.

children.label: Purpose & Operating Model
children.notes: Purple teaming validates hypotheses about controls against realistic behaviors, reveals why gaps exist, transfers knowledge in both directions, and creates repeatable tests. When defenders know every step in advance, describe the work as collaborative validation rather than a stealth assessment. Preserve independent red-team testing when the assurance question requires it.

children.label: Purple-Team Roles
children.notes: The facilitator defines objectives, safety, learning goals, and the debrief. An emulation engineer produces controlled behavior and evidence. Detection engineers, hunters, and responders inspect visibility and decisions. Threat intelligence supplies context. Platform, control, asset, and risk owners ensure findings become implemented changes.

children.label: Facilitator / Lead
children.notes: Creates a fair test, manages safety and communication, keeps red and blue aligned on evidence, distinguishes learning exercises from assurance assessments, and turns observations into owned improvements.

children.label: Emulation Engineer
children.notes: Translates a threat behavior into a safe atomic or chained test, documents prerequisites and expected artifacts, executes consistently, and preserves a reusable test fixture.

children.label: Detection Validation
children.notes: Detection engineers, hunters, and responders trace activity from raw telemetry through enrichment, analytics, alert routing, triage, decisions, and response. They improve behavior-based coverage without tuning only to a test string.

children.label: Validation Loop
children.notes: Prioritize a threat-informed, business-relevant behavior; define expected prevention, telemetry, detection, triage, and response; execute the minimum safe test; compare observed evidence with expectations; classify the gap; assign an owner; improve the control; rerun the same test; and preserve it for regression.

children.label: Methods & Shared Language
children.notes: Use threat intelligence and threat modeling to select scenarios. A common technique framework such as MITRE ATT&CK helps teams communicate, but it is not a checklist and a colorful heatmap is not proof of capability. Practitioners need offensive safety, telemetry pipelines, detection logic, query testing, incident workflows, control engineering, automation, experiment design, and blameless facilitation.

children.label: Outputs & Measures
children.notes: Outputs include emulation plans, safety controls, detection-as-code, test fixtures, telemetry requirements, coverage evidence, gap tickets, joint reports, owners, and regression schedules. Measure tests producing usable telemetry, tests triggering high-quality detections, analyst decision quality, time to detect or contain, gap closure and retest rate, and recurring failures. Coverage needs asset, platform, data source, analytic quality, test date, result, owner, and response context.

children.label: How They Work Together
children.notes: Red supplies controlled adversary behavior, blue supplies prevention, telemetry, investigation, and response, and purple structures the shared experiment. Together they operate a continuous cycle from risk hypothesis to verified improvement. The teams share evidence and accountability while retaining independence when an assurance objective requires a blind test.

children.label: 1. Prioritize Risk
children.notes: Use business impact, asset criticality, architecture, incident history, and threat intelligence to form a testable hypothesis: if behavior X occurs against asset Y, control Z should prevent or detect it and responders should act within an agreed time.

children.label: 2. Scope Safely
children.notes: Agree targets, identities, techniques, timing, disclosure to defenders, evidence, communications, cleanup, rollback, exclusions, success criteria, and stop conditions. Confirm authorization and third-party or cloud constraints before touching a system.

children.label: 3. Emulate
children.notes: Red performs the minimum controlled and attributable behavior needed to answer the hypothesis. Start with atomic tests and chain behaviors only when required. Record exact times, source, target, identity, action, expected telemetry, and cleanup.

children.label: 4. Observe & Respond
children.notes: Blue checks prevention, raw telemetry, enrichment, analytics, alert delivery, triage, analyst reasoning, containment, recovery, and communications. Record the first point where actual behavior diverges from the expected path.

children.label: 5. Debrief
children.notes: Red explains intent and execution, blue explains visibility and decisions, and purple aligns the evidence. Use a blameless expected-versus-observed review to separate missing telemetry, pipeline failure, weak analytics, routing, playbook, skill, and preventive-control gaps. Record successes as well as failures.

children.label: 6. Fix & Tune
children.notes: Improve configuration, architecture, logging, analytics, enrichment, playbooks, training, or risk treatment. Prefer durable behavior-based controls and root-cause fixes over brittle indicators. Assign an owner, acceptance evidence, deadline, operational-impact review, and rollback plan.

children.label: 7. Retest & Measure
children.notes: Rerun the same behavior, confirm the expected result end to end, and preserve the scenario as a regression test. Feed lessons into architecture, threat models, detections, response plans, training, future engagements, and leadership risk decisions. A claimed fix is not trusted until the agreed evidence confirms it.

children.label: Learning & Career Roadmap
children.notes: Start broad, practice legally, choose a first lens, and prove your reasoning with a portfolio. Certifications can help with structure or hiring filters, but they are optional and should match the role and local job market. Demonstrated fundamentals, safe judgment, clear writing, and curiosity remain essential.

children.label: 1. Build the Base
children.notes: Learn networking, Linux, Windows, identity, web and API behavior, cloud basics, scripting, Git, risk concepts, common controls, and incident fundamentals. Be able to explain normal system behavior before diagnosing malicious behavior.

children.label: 2. Build a Legal Lab
children.notes: Create an isolated environment with intentionally vulnerable targets and a separate logging system. Generate activity, capture packets, read endpoint and identity logs, harden a host, validate a known weakness, restore the environment, and document the safety boundaries.

children.label: Red Portfolio Project
children.notes: Assess an intentionally vulnerable web application or small lab under written rules of engagement. Produce a sanitized report with evidence, an attack path, impact, root cause, prioritized remediation, cleanup, and verification. Manual understanding matters more than running many tools.

children.label: Blue Portfolio Project
children.notes: Collect endpoint, authentication, and network events; generate a benign suspicious sequence; trace it through the log pipeline; write and test a detection; document triage and containment; measure false positives; and add a small incident playbook.

children.label: Purple Portfolio Project
children.notes: Select one harmless adversary behavior, define expected controls and data sources, emulate it safely, verify the full path to an analyst-visible result, improve the detection, and store the test, query, evidence, and retest checklist together in version control.

children.label: Entry Roles & Bridges
children.notes: Help desk, system or network administration, software development, QA, cloud operations, data analysis, audit, risk, and compliance can all lead into security because they build system, user, operational, or business context. Search for responsibilities and mentorship rather than relying only on job titles.

children.label: Prove the Work
children.notes: Publish sanitized reports, diagrams, scripts, detection rules, test fixtures, playbooks, and lessons learned. Explain assumptions, failed approaches, evidence, impact, remediation, tradeoffs, and ethical boundaries. Never publish secrets, personal data, client evidence, or working access to real systems.

children.label: Durable Human Skills
children.notes: Develop investigative skepticism, systems thinking, threat modeling, experiment design, technical writing, facilitation, empathy, prioritization, ethics, and business communication. These skills connect tool output to trustworthy decisions and become more valuable as routine work is automated.

children.label: AI Impact
children.notes: AI changes the speed, scale, and attack surface of cybersecurity. It can accelerate legitimate work and adversary activity, but it does not remove the need for authorization, evidence, domain knowledge, privacy controls, or human accountability. Treat model output as untrusted until verified.

children.label: Attackers & Red Teams
children.notes: AI can accelerate reconnaissance, code comprehension, test generation, language adaptation, social-engineering variation, exploit prototyping, and tool orchestration. Defenders should expect more convincing content, faster iteration, and attacks targeting AI-enabled workflows. Authorized red teams can model those risks, but every generated claim, payload, and action requires verification and scope control.

children.label: Blue-Team Augmentation
children.notes: AI can summarize alerts, translate queries, correlate context, explain code, cluster cases, draft playbooks, assist malware analysis, suggest competing hypotheses, and reduce repetitive work. Risks include automation bias, missed nuance, fabricated evidence, model drift, data leakage, and prompt injection hidden in logs, emails, tickets, or retrieved documents.

children.label: Purple-Team Augmentation
children.notes: AI can help map behaviors to candidate data sources, propose safe test variations, generate synthetic telemetry, compare expected and observed evidence, draft detection logic, and organize coverage gaps. Purple teams should validate every mapping, query, assumption, and result empirically and keep tests reproducible outside the model conversation.

children.label: New AI Attack Surface
children.notes: Threat-model the model, prompts, training and retrieval data, application, users, tools, agents, identities, infrastructure, providers, and software supply chain as one system. Key risks include prompt injection, insecure tool use, excessive agency, sensitive-data disclosure, poisoned training or retrieval data, model theft, model evasion, insecure output handling, denial of service, dependency compromise, and weak tenant isolation.

children.label: Controls for AI Systems
children.notes: Apply strong identity, least-privileged tools, sandboxing, network and action allowlists, input and output validation, data classification, secret isolation, provenance, rate and cost limits, monitoring, human approval for consequential actions, rollback, dependency controls, adversarial testing, and incident playbooks. Test ordinary software security and AI-specific behavior together.

children.label: Safe AI Use in Security
children.notes: Use only approved models and data paths. Do not paste secrets, proprietary code, personal data, malware samples, or client evidence into an unapproved service. Constrain tools and permissions, log prompts and actions where policy allows, verify sources and raw telemetry, require human approval for blocking, deleting, containing, notifying, or changing production, and maintain a tested rollback path.

children.label: Evaluation & Governance
children.notes: Maintain an inventory of models, versions, data sources, agents, tools, owners, and permitted uses. Define privacy, quality, safety, cost, and security criteria; test adversarial and ordinary cases; monitor drift and failures; preserve auditability; and decide when human review is mandatory. A convincing demonstration is not the same as a reliable production control.

children.label: The Human Advantage
children.notes: AI raises the value of judgment, threat modeling, skepticism, systems thinking, experiment design, ethical reasoning, communication, and business context. Use AI to accelerate bounded work, while humans remain responsible for authorization, interpretation, risk acceptance, and consequential decisions.
